Fall

Bridget Riley’s 1963 painting of a single wave line repeated across the surface, with waves that tighten toward the bottom until the field seems to ripple.

Source
Tate: Bridget Riley, “Fall”, T00616
Creator
Bridget Riley
Made

Style

Moods
Vibrating, disorienting, precise
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected Tate’s image of T00616 (1196 × 1200 px) from media.tate.org.uk in a scratchpad. The artwork page renders most of its text with JavaScript; the medium was read from the page metadata. No image is stored.

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Tate lists Fall, 1963, as polyvinyl acetate paint on hardboard, collection number T00616, on display at Tate Britain in the Bridget Riley room. Tate.

Riley’s Current (1964), a painting of the same kind, was reproduced on the cover of The Responsive Eye catalogue in 1965. David Zwirner.

Observed

  • Thin vertical black and white stripes of almost equal width fill the square surface to all four edges.
  • Every stripe follows the same wavy path. In the upper part the waves are long and gentle; toward the bottom they become shorter and sharper.
  • In the lowest band the waves are so tight that the stripes seem to vibrate and form moiré-like ridges.
  • The black is slightly warm and the white slightly off-white in the photograph. There is no other colour and no texture beyond the paint.

Why it belongs

Fall is the reference case for the style’s “progression and distortion” grammar: nothing changes except the period of one repeated curve.

It shows why op patterns need a fixed size on screen: the effect depends on the width of each stripe relative to the eye.

Borrow

Repeat one wave path hundreds of times with a small horizontal offset, and shorten its period toward one edge.

Fill the whole panel edge to edge so that the field has no frame inside it.
